qti-choice-interaction.qti-prompt: After reviewing years of properly run clinical trials, the national medicines regulator praises the research team's work but calls the evidence incomplete. It announces it will make no ruling on the new allergy treatment until a two-year follow-up study concludes; until then, the treatment cannot be sold. Which statement best describes the regulator's action?
qti-choice-interaction.qti-simple-choice: The regulator sanctioned the treatment, formally approving its sale.
The regulator recalled the treatment, ordering it pulled from every pharmacy shelf.
The regulator fined the manufacturer, punishing it for skipping the required trials.
The regulator shelved the application, putting off any ruling for years.

qti-content-body.p: Exactly. The regulator set the application aside -- no approval, no rejection, no penalty -- and will not return to it until the two-year follow-up study is finished. Putting off a decision like that is shelving it.

Pin down what the regulator actually decided: nothing, on purpose. It granted no permission to sell, so the treatment was not approved; the treatment has never been on pharmacy shelves, so there was nothing to pull back; and the trials were properly run and even praised, so no one was punished. Which statement names setting a decision aside until more data arrives?

Sanction cuts two ways -- official approval, or a penalty that enforces a rule -- and the regulator did neither. It expressly announced it would make no ruling, so nothing was approved; and with the trials properly run and praised, there was no violation to punish. Praise is not permission: an application set aside for two more years of data has been shelved, not sanctioned in either sense.

Recalling a product means ordering it pulled from shelves it is already on. This treatment has never been sold -- the regulator's announcement is precisely that it cannot go on sale yet. You cannot pull back what was never released.

A fine would punish wrongdoing, but the scenario rules that out twice: the trials were properly run, and the regulator went out of its way to praise the research team. The evidence was incomplete, not improper -- a reason to wait, not to punish.
